summary: Gereaux Island light, first shown in 1870 at the entrance to Byng Inlet on Georgian Bay, has a square wooden tower built in 1880; it is now a Coast Guard station.

access.note: Accessible only by boat. Site and tower closed (Lighthouse Directory). Coast Guard property.

events.note: Sawmill companies at Byng Inlet erect a lighthouse on a small island at the entrance, without waiting for plans; the Department of Marine finds it unsafe in high winds (LighthouseFriends)

Station established 1870 (LighthouseFriends; Lighthouse Directory). The sawmill companies' first tower was built in 1869 (LighthouseFriends), so the 1870 date is the station date, not the building date.
Sawmill company operated the light until 1 May 1875, when the Department of Marine took over
Present square tapered tower with attached dwelling built by P.J. Sylvester to Department of Marine designs under Chief Lighthouse Engineer Joseph Tomlinson; replaces the lumber-company tower
Fixed white light, 47 ft above the water, placed in operation October 1880
Range lights placed in operation shortly after the opening of navigation: front light fixed red, back light fixed white

In the year ended 31 March 1911 (lights list): fourth-order lens, petroleum vapour under a mantle, replaces the five mammoth lamps and reflectors of the catoptric apparatus. The 'remains fixed white' sentence in that volume belongs to the Burlington bay entry, not this one.
Byng Inlet range works recorded in the Department's new aids list: combined dwelling and tower for the front light; steel skeleton tower for the back light
Steamer Greenville aground on Burton Bank in a snowstorm in December 1924 while searching for the island light, which was out (LighthouseFriends only)
Skeletal tower replaces the wooden back light of the Byng Inlet range, which had served since 1890; the island light is shown from a skeletal tower for at least twenty years (LighthouseFriends)
Detached keeper's bungalow added for an extra keeper to run a new foghorn and radiobeacon
Lighthouse and range lights automated, when Art Niederhumer's service ended
Recognized Federal Heritage Building, 5 September 1991 (register entry 9678)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1990 federal heritage statement says the light was no longer operational. The Coast Guard's current list gives it as operating (Oc W 10s), and the Lighthouse Directory calls it active. LighthouseFriends says the light had been shown from a skeletal tower for at least twenty years and is now back inside the historic tower, with no date for the return. The record's active status matches the current list.

The Department's list for the year ended 31 March 1912 records a steel skeleton tower for the back light. LighthouseFriends dates a skeletal back tower to 1936 and says the wooden back tower had served since 1890. The two accounts are not reconciled in the sources and are left open for a human check.
LighthouseFriends prints the first keeper as Joseph Lamondin; the 1876 report as quoted by LighthouseFriends prints Joseph Lamondet. The story uses Lamondin and notes the variant.
The Lighthouse Directory gives 14 m (45 ft); the Coast Guard list and LighthouseFriends give 15.1 m. The story uses 15.1 m.
The Lighthouse Directory gives 16 m; the Coast Guard list and LighthouseFriends give 15.9 m. The story uses 15.9 m from the Coast Guard list.

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-27: all 75 quotes were found on the first run, but one was misattributed and is removed from the story. The 1911 lights list sentence 'The light remains fixed white' is at the end of the Burlington bay entry (scan p. 84 neighbourhood), not the Gercaux island entry, which says only that the five mammoth lamps were replaced by a 4th order lens and burns petroleum vapour under a mantle. The story no longer quotes 'remains fixed white'. Story changes: the 1911 change is stated for the year ended 31 March 1911; the station is dated 1870 with the 1869 sawmill tower noted (LighthouseFriends); the 1880, 1900 and 1876-era distances and heights are metres first (14 m (47 ft), 10 m (34 ft), 18 m (60 ft), 5.5 by 6.1 m (18 by 20 ft)); the 1923 'Grenville' is no longer presented as the same vessel as the 1924 'Greenville' (the spelling differs and the sources do not connect them); the heritage statement's no-longer-operational view is set against the current list. Page checks: the 1911 lights list is scan p. 84 (the printed page is unconfirmed and not cited); the 1911 keepers list is scan p. 253 printed p. 246, matched by row (name and date on one OCR line; the station is not on that line); the 1914 list is scan p. 74 printed p. 67 and 'Byng inlet (3 lights)' and 'L. Lamondin' are on one OCR line; the 1912 Byng inlet entry is scan p. 58 (confirmed, 'Establishment of range lights ... forming the front light ... steel skeleton tower, for the back light'); the 1923 'Grenville' is scan p. 112 (confirmed; the 1923 volume also has the steamer at scan p. 110). The Louis Lamondin row (1911, scan p. 253) was NOT checked against the page image: a human must confirm that the row is Byng inlet before the story treats it as the station's keeper appointment. The 1900 range description and the 1876 report remain cited as LighthouseFriends quotes them. Earlier note follows. The 1876 report and the 1900 range-light description are not in the corpus (it starts in 1900 and holds no 1876 volume), so both are cited as LighthouseFriends quotes them. The 1900 range description is a LighthouseFriends quotation of the 1900 report; the corpus grep did not find the passage. The Grenville/Greenville name: the Department's reports spell the Dominion steamer Grenville; LighthouseFriends prints Greenville. The December 1924 grounding rests on LighthouseFriends alone: the Department's 1924 volume (year ended 31 March 1924) stops before December 1924, and the corpus has no volume for the year ended 31 March 1925. The 1912 range works and the 1936 skeletal tower do not agree (see resolved_conflicts); a human should check scan p. 58 of the 1912 volume and the LighthouseFriends source. The 1990 heritage statement's 'no longer operational' predates the current list; its date is not printed, and its bottom date stamp reads 1994.12.05. The Heritage Guide page gives the register as Built 1880 and recognized 5 September 1991 and cites a 1990 FHBRO report; the statement itself is dated only by its report number. Keepers after 1946 come from the LighthouseFriends roster only; the Department's 1914 and 1911 lists confirm Louis Lamondin, and the 1909 Ontario list shows Louis Lamondin in place. Art Niederhumer's connection ended in 1989; he is named in his public role only. Charles Lamondin's dismissal comes from LighthouseFriends alone. OCR: the 1911 report prints 'Gercaux island' for Gereaux Island (scan p. 84 is confirmed; the printed page is marked '?', so the printed page is not used). The 1912 scan p. 58 printed page is also unconfirmed, so only the scan page is cited. No newspaper search was run for this station. The Lighthouse Directory's 'Parry Sound District Lighthouses' heading supports the district name in the record.
